transcript:
Header: 2026-07-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Daniel (ArborPay), Priya (ArborPay), Samir (ArborPay)

Summary: quick review of last week's throughput runs, tuning knobs (batch cap, concurrency, queue depth), and next steps for the on-prem run

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh real quick can we do roll call?
[00:08] Daniel: yeah this is Daniel, platform eng at ArborPay, Priya and Samir are here too, hi
[00:12] Priya: Priya here
[00:14] Samir: Samir, CTO
[00:16] Maya: great, Liam and I from Redwood, quick agenda - results, tuning notes, and plan for the on-prem run
[00:30] Liam: ok so ran the 4-hour test with continuous batching enabled. baseline (no batching) was ~1.1k rps with avg token latency ~90ms but p99 around 420ms under our synthetic mix
[00:48] Daniel: sorry can you say p99 again?
[00:50] Liam: p99 ~420ms, yeah - with continuous batching turned on and batch cap 32 we saw throughput jump to 1.9k rps but p99 moved to ~610ms when concurrency spiked above 100
[01:10] Priya: that matches what we saw in prod-ish traffic - big tails when spikes occur, we're trying to keep 95th < 250ms
[01:20] Maya: ok important signal - so tradeoff clear: batching increases tokens/sec but worsens tail latency at high concurrency. we should find operational concurrency target where batching gives gain without unacceptable tail
[01:36] Liam: right, strategy we're recommending: set a concurrency soft cap and a small request queue with admission control. if queue depth > X then fall back to smaller batch cap or route to a lower-cost model variant - keep callers happy
[01:52] Daniel: when you say queue depth, is that server-side queueing or client-side?
[01:55] Liam: server-side queueing in the runtime we run, so it's per-worker. we can expose metrics so you can see queue build-up; also we can do circuit breaker thresholds
[02:08] Samir: how deterministic is the batching schedule - we don't want jitter that causes other services to time out
[02:14] Liam: batching is opportunistic and continuous - we pack tokens as they arrive up to batch cap or latency cutoff (we set 15ms as a hard cap in tests). there is small additional jitter but we tune the latency cutoff to bound that
[02:28] Priya: can you remind us of the latency cutoff you used?
[02:31] Liam: we used 15ms in the 4-hour run, and also did a run with 8ms - with 8ms the throughput gain was smaller (1.4k rps) but p99 improved to ~330ms
[02:43] Daniel: so 8ms cut helps tails but loses some throughput. can we do dynamic cutoff based on CPU and queue levels?
[02:50] Liam: yes, we've got heuristics - adjust cutoff based on worker queue utilization. that's in our autoscaling/optimizer roadmap
[03:02] Maya: action item - Liam will run a 6-hour with concurrency target 80 and another at 120 so we can see headroom and cost deltas
[03:09] Liam: yep will do
[03:12] [03:12] Liam: quick note on KV/prefix caching - prefix cache reduced repeated prompt cost by 18% on average in this workload, but caching hit rate depends heavily on prompt normalization
[03:28] Priya: our input variance is high, how invasive is prompt normalization? we can do light normalization but not deep rewrite
[03:35] Liam: light normalization (strip timestamps, normalize UUIDs) gives most of the hit. we're not doing semantic rewriting, just canonicalization
[03:44] Daniel: any security/practical concerns with caching? we need to ensure no PII is cached and that cache is encrypted per-customer
[03:51] Maya: yes we support per-tenant KV with encryption at rest and access controls; we can also disable cache per route
[03:57] Samir: ok good, that meets compliance bar for us for now
[04:03] [04:03] Liam: another observation - when we increased concurrency beyond worker pool size, queueing time increased linearly and you start to see long tails; recommended to keep headroom of ~1.3x worker capacity to absorb spikes
[04:18] Priya: what worker pool size are you using in the test?
[04:21] Liam: 16 workers per server, each worker has its own queue. worker-level concurrency is 8 requests in flight for transformer KV usage; overall target concurrency we reported is 128 across the cluster
[04:33] Daniel: can you map that to the Dedicated config we were looking at?
[04:36] Maya: yes - for your Dedicated plan with 4 GPU nodes that maps to roughly 3.8k rps baseline without batching; with batching and tuned caps you can get to ~6k rps but costs go up and tails require careful routing
[04:50] Samir: cost is a big lever for us - we're trying to avoid 2x cost for marginal perf gains
[04:57] Liam: totally - we included cost-per-1k-tokens in the spreadsheet. for example, enabling continuous batching with cap 32 reduced per-token cost by ~26%, but once you add extra capacity to tame p99 the net cost benefit shrinks to ~8%
[05:12] Daniel: so we need the sweet spot for our SLOs and cost target. can you put up the numbers again?
[05:18] Maya: I'll share the spreadsheet after this call - it shows throughput, p95, p99, and cost for the matrix we ran: batch caps 8/16/32, concurrency 50/80/120
[05:29] Priya: another variable is quantization and kernel selection - are you using int8 quant in these runs?
[05:34] Liam: yes Q4 int8 on the public run; on the on-prem we can test Q2/Q4 mixes. kernel selection was auto chosen by runtime, we saw better perf with custom fused attention on our test infra
[05:46] Samir: will quantization change inference stability or correctness? we're sensitive about hallucination rate
[05:51] Liam: for the family of models you're testing, we did a quick eval - int8 had negligible quality drop on our eval set; we still recommend running your regression prompts though
[06:03] Daniel: ok we will run regression set in parallel
[06:07] [06:07] Maya: good. next, about routing and fallback - if queue depth hits threshold we can route to a cheaper model variant with lower token length or to hosted fallback region
[06:20] Priya: fallback region - do you support cross-region replication for KV?
[06:24] Liam: yes, but replication adds ~20ms. for strict latency targets you want regional caches. for resiliency we replicate async
[06:33] Daniel: any recommended monitoring dashboards to catch queues before they hurt SLOs?
[06:37] Maya: we ship dashboards with per-worker queue depth, batch size histograms, and end-to-end p95/p99 traces. we can give you alert thresholds for 1m spike and sustained 5m window
[06:49] Priya: perfect, send alert recommendations
[06:51] Maya: will do
[06:53] [10:00] Liam: jumping forward - we observed that tail latency correlates strongly with burstiness of short requests (few tokens). when you have a mix of long and short inputs, batching can actually help short ones if you do preferential batching by token length
[10:20] Daniel: preferential batching?
[10:22] Liam: separate micro-queues for short vs long; batch short together aggressively, keep a small cap for long so they don't blow up batch assembly time
[10:31] Priya: that seems useful, our distribution is 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long
[10:36] Liam: perfect, that distribution will benefit from preferential batching - will include in next test set
[10:40] [18:00] Maya: quick check - are there any network/security blockers for the on-prem run?
[18:06] Daniel: we need to confirm peering and CA cert exchange, also our networking team needs a contact
[18:11] Maya: Daniel, please share contact, we'll loop in our infra eng to coordinate
[18:15] Daniel: will do, action item logged
[18:18] [25:00] Liam: timeline - I propose we run the 6-hour continuous-batching tests in our lab by Friday, share raw logs, then you'll run a brief on-prem smoke during the pilot week.
[25:12] Priya: that works for us, need to align with our release freeze next Tuesday but pilot week after that is fine
[25:20] Maya: ok noted, we'll tentatively schedule pilot week 2026-07-20
[25:25] [33:00] Maya: final recap - Liam runs the two long tests (concurrency 80 and 120) and posts logs and flamegraphs, I share spreadsheet and alert thresholds, Priya sends traffic dump and SLOs, Daniel confirms peering window and contact.
[33:20] Samir: that captures it, thanks all
[33:25] Daniel: quick question on SLOs - we'll target 95th <250ms and p99 <600ms for user-facing endpoints, is that acceptable?
[33:35] Maya: yes that's achievable with the tuned configs and modest extra capacity, we'll put numbers in the spreadsheet
[33:42] Priya: please also add cost delta per 1k queries so we can present to finance
[33:47] Liam: will include cost column - approximated for Hosted vs Dedicated
[40:00] Maya: ok wrapping up, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule.
[40:08] Daniel: thanks, bye
[40:10] Priya: thanks all
[40:12] Samir: bye

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard terms (e.g., K V cache as spelled out) and some speaker overlap. Links referenced: shared spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/arborpay-throughput), security docs (link: https://redwood.example.com/security/arborpay-soc2)
